turns.text: Explain our workforce position in plain terms — pretend I'm a brand-new dean.

Here's the lay of the land for San Mateo County CCD in Advanced Manufacturing. You're a district of 3 colleges in the Bay Area, so everything below is at the district level. The regional picture first: Bay Area employers are projected to have about 8,150 job openings a year in this field (Centers of Excellence, 2024–2029). All 26 colleges in the region combined turn out roughly 3,900 completers a year, which leaves a regional gap of about 4,227 openings a year the region's colleges don't currently supply into. Your district's share of that: you produce about 200 completers a year — roughly 1 in 20 (about 5%) of the region's supply — through 2 programs in this sector. Electronics and Electric Technology puts out about 10 completers a year and prepares students for 8 occupations carrying roughly 1,170 openings a year across the region; Energy Systems Technology puts out about 11 a year and prepares students for 5 occupations with roughly 1,000 openings. The sector as a whole spans 49 occupations. Two caveats worth holding: supply is a 3-year average of completions, so a single recent year can run a bit above or below it, and the demand figure is the whole region's, not demand reserved for your graduates.

Plainest version: Bay Area employers want about 8,150 people a year for these manufacturing jobs. Every college in the region combined only trains about 3,900 — so roughly 4,200 openings a year go unfilled. Your district trains about 200 of them, about 1 in 20 of the region's total, through 2 programs.
Bay Area manufacturing has about 4,200 more job openings a year than the region's colleges fill, and your district supplies about 1 in 20 of the region's trained workers.
